source.title: Survival of the Fittest Representation: A Case Study with Modular Addition
source.authors: Xiaoman Delores Ding; Zifan Carl Guo; Eric J. Michaud; Zi-Ming Liu; Max Tegmark

page_placements.theme: Initialization predicts feature selection and acquisition order

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tracks Fourier-frequency representations during modular-addition training and tests how retaining or ablating circles affects task performance. It does not directly measure delayed train/test accuracy or test the complete grokking account.
record.gate_note: The paper reports many additional results about which initial signals, gradients, embedding dimensions, and weight-decay settings predict the number or identity of surviving circles. Those results do not measure the delayed generalization behavior named in the claim versions, so they are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses the known Fourier-circle representation of modular addition as a tool to study competition between circles. It measures circle signals, which circles survive, and test loss under circle ablations. It never reports train versus test accuracy over time, a delayed generalization jump, or its timing. Weight decay is set to 0.5 so the model 'quickly groks.' None of its results show whether a grokking version holds, so it does not test the claim. Its findings are listed under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that modular-addition embeddings decompose into frequency-specific circles that compete under resource constraints, set by embedding dimension and weight decay. Circles with large initial signals and gradients are more likely to survive, and more circles survive as the embedding dimension grows. Circles cooperate to reduce loss, and their signal dynamics are described by a simple linear differential equation.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than measuring delayed train/test accuracy as in the original grokking recipe, the study analyzes Fourier-frequency representations, their survival, and circle-ablation effects in modular addition.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported number of surviving circles changes with embedding dimension and weight decay; circle-ablation outcomes also differ between well-initialized and randomly selected frequencies.

fits_no_version.finding: Fourier circles compete during training. Survival rate correlates with initial signal (Pearson 0.85, p<1e-3), and perturbing one frequency's initial signal changes its survival. An SVM on initial signal and gradient separates surviving from dead frequencies with 83.8% accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Which Fourier frequencies a modular-addition network learns is predictable from their initial signal and gradient.

fits_no_version.finding: The number of surviving circles rises with embedding dimension d and modulus p, and falls as weight decay increases. With weight decay 0, all frequencies survive and the network fails to generalize; no numbers are given in the text.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representation redundancy (circle count) in modular addition is set by embedding capacity and weight decay.

fits_no_version.finding: Circles cooperate. One circle fails, two random circles struggle, and three reach near-zero loss. Two well-initialized circles (the strongest frequencies from an unablated run) reach test loss around 1e-7. A single-circle solution never formed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Trained modular-addition networks use multiple cooperating circles rather than a single-frequency clock algorithm.

fits_no_version.finding: Circle-signal dynamics over the first 1000 steps are fit well by a sparse linear ODE (R^2 near 1 for linear regression; Lasso comparable).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early representation dynamics of Fourier components follow simple linear interactions.

record.problems: The study focuses on one toy task, modular addition. It does not directly measure train accuracy, delayed test-accuracy improvement, or whether circle-signal measures anticipate a generalization jump. Several plotted outcomes are described without numerical values.
record.rows_left_out: Results on initial-signal and initial-gradient predictors, embedding-dimension sweeps, weight-decay sweeps, and ODE-fit quality were left out because they do not measure the delayed-generalization behavior or the specific gradual generalizing-circuit outcome in the versions tested.

untested.parts: No train-accuracy saturation, delayed test-accuracy jump, or training-set-size effect on delay is reported; the split is fixed at 80-20.
Circle signals are tracked, but not against the timing of a generalization jump. Memorizing components are neither identified nor shown to be removed.
No non-algorithmic data and no initialization-scale or lazy-to-rich test of grokking. The lazy regime is only speculated about for frozen embeddings.
Weight decay is varied only against the number of surviving circles. There is no critical dataset size, no ungrokking, and no efficiency comparison.
Survival of different frequencies and different numbers of circles across runs is reported. Whether runs learn the same or different algorithms (e.g. clock versus pizza) is not examined.
Adam-linked slingshot loss spikes are noted but explicitly left outside scope. There are no optimizer or numerical controls.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's guess of 'tests/T2' with a V2 'supports' label is not justified. The study only mentions grokking in passing (weight decay chosen so the model 'quickly groks') and never measures delayed generalization or relates circle signals to a test-accuracy jump. All rows are relinked to none. Training uses AdamW, learning rate 0.01, 3e4 steps, and a 2-hidden-layer MLP of width 100.

versions.untested_parts: No train-accuracy saturation, chance-level test accuracy, delayed rise in test accuracy, or effect of training-set size on delay is reported.

The study tracks Fourier-circle signals and tests circle ablations, but does not show that a generalizing circuit forms before a test-accuracy jump, that memorizing components are removed, or that continuous measures anticipate such a jump.
No non-algorithmic data, initialization-scale sweep, or lazy-to-rich transition test is reported.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is studied.
Weight decay is varied in relation to circle counts, but the study does not test the efficiency account, critical dataset size, or ungrokking.
The study does not identify and compare the algorithms learned across runs, architectures, or hyperparameters.
The study mentions Adam-associated slingshot behavior but does not control optimizer or numerical choices to test whether grokking delays are artifacts.

rows.subject: modular-addition embedding-MLP model
rows.size_stated: p = 59, d = 128; two hidden layers of 100 neurons each
rows.operation_detail: Tracked Fourier signal magnitudes and projected embeddings for frequencies during training.
rows.measure: Fourier signal magnitude and projected-circle formation over training
rows.value: The text reports that surviving frequencies separate from the others, whose signals quickly go to almost zero; surviving-frequency projections stabilize into circles while dead-frequency projections collapse toward the center.
rows.note: This documents changing representation signals, but does not establish that they anticipate a delayed test-accuracy jump or distinguish generalizing from memorizing components.
rows.check: Fourier signal trajectories are not aligned with any train/test accuracy curve or generalization jump. Dead frequencies are non-surviving Fourier components, not memorizing components, so the row cannot show V2's anticipation claim.

relation.reason: Chooses a training setup intended to grok, then measures Fourier-circle survival and interactions without directly testing a listed claim version.

tranche.reason: Uses established modular-addition circle representations to study representation competition; does not establish delayed generalization, its anticipation by progress measures, or distinct learned algorithms across runs.

source_check.notes: The synthesis statement is supported by Section 3.2.1 and Figure 6, rather than its cited R1, which describes Figure 2 trajectories. Non-surviving Fourier components are not identified as memorizing components.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Modular-addition Fourier-circle trajectories and circle-ablation experiments
reader_labels.reason: The text reports dead-circle signal decay, surviving circles stabilizing, and task performance depending on which circles are retained; this supports a representation-dynamics component of the version, but not the full delayed-jump account (R1-R8).
